practice.title: Implement Depth-First Search
practice.statementHtml: For a complete DFS forest, read graph in 0–3 and the first root start in 0–5. Use the undirected connections and cyclic root convention described above. Print each vertex letter, discovery time, finish time and component id. Then print components followed by its count. Start time at zero and component ids at zero. For this Depth-First Search solution, the first output line is Enter graph (0-3) and start (0-5):. Vertex indices are A=0 through F=5.
hints: সব পাশের নোড দেখা শেষে বের হওয়ার সময় রাখো।

practice.title: A full DFS forest beginning at F
practice.statementHtml: Select the DFS test graph using one integer from 0 through 3. This exercise fixes the initial root at F. Begin the root order at F, then wrap to A through E. Print each letter, discovery time, finish time and component id, followed by components and its count. The clock begins at zero and component ids begin at zero. Neighbours use ascending order. Begin the A full DFS forest beginning at F output with Enter graph (0-3); start is F:. Vertex indices are A=0 through F=5.
hints: যে এজ দিয়ে ঢুকেছ, তার উল্টো দিকটা নতুন সাইকেল নয়।

practice.title: Nested times on the common graph by hand
practice.statementHtml: Trace the recursive DFS from A in graph 0 with ascending neighbours. Give every discovery and finish time, the deepest active stack, and the component count.
hints: চাইল্ডের ঢোকা ও বের হওয়ার সময় প্যারেন্টের সময়ের ভেতরে থাকে।
practice.answerHtml:
Starting at A produces the recursive path A, B, C, E, D, F before any return. The first completed call is F. Then D returns to E, E returns to C, and the remaining callers finish in reverse nesting order.

VertexDiscoveryFinishComponent
A1120
B2110
C3100
D580
E490
F670

The interval for C is [3,10], and the interval for E is [4,9]. One contains the other because E is a descendant of C. Intervals belonging to separate DFS trees are disjoint. Discovery order alone would not tell you when a vertex stopped being active.

practice.title: Every call completes its reachable white region by hand
practice.statementHtml: Prove that a recursive DFS call finishes exactly after its descendants, and that complete outer restarts partition an undirected graph into components.
hints: চাইল্ডের ঢোকা ও বের হওয়ার সময় প্যারেন্টের সময়ের ভেতরে থাকে।
practice.answerHtml:
During a DFS call, every active vertex is on the current recursion path. A newly called vertex was white, so a vertex cannot create a second active call for itself. This discovery rule prevents infinite recursion around cycles. Each call has a finite neighbour list and eventually returns.

If an edge leaves a discovered vertex toward a white neighbour, DFS follows it before that vertex finishes. Suppose some reachable vertex stayed white after the root returned. Along a path from the root, take the first white vertex. Its predecessor was explored and should have followed that edge, which is a contradiction.

In an undirected graph, one root therefore visits exactly one connected component. No edge can lead into another component by definition. Restarting at a white vertex selects a different component, so the outer loop partitions all vertices correctly. This argument does not establish strongly connected components for directed graphs.

quiz.prompt: What does a grey DFS vertex represent?
quiz.explanation: Grey vertices lie on the current call stack.

quiz.prompt: When is finish[u] assigned in recursive DFS?
options: After all outgoing neighbour inspections finish
quiz.explanation: Finish records returning from u, after descendants complete.

quiz.prompt: Which timestamp relation identifies a proper DFS descendant v of u?
quiz.explanation: Recursive calls nest their entry and exit intervals.

quiz.prompt: Why does undirected DFS skip the exact reverse tree edge for cycle evidence?
options: It is the same physical edge used to enter the child
quiz.explanation: A second view of one tree edge does not form a new simple cycle.

quiz.prompt: What does each new outer DFS root count in an undirected graph?
options: One strongly connected component of any directed graph
quiz.explanation: A complete undirected search exhausts exactly its root component.

quiz.prompt: What is the worst-case recursive depth of DFS on V vertices?
quiz.explanation: A chain can discover every vertex before any call returns.

quiz.prompt: What additional distinction is needed beyond tree/back/finished in directed classification?
options: Treat every black neighbour as a back edge
Separate forward from cross edges among finished destinations
quiz.explanation: Ancestor intervals distinguish a completed descendant from another branch.

quiz.prompt: What finish time does the DFS root receive on a three-node chain?
quiz.explanation: Three discoveries occur before the three nested returns; the root finishes last at six.

quiz.prompt: At what clock value is the deepest chain vertex discovered?
quiz.explanation: The calls enter 0, then 1, then 2, so the third vertex is discovered at three.

quiz.prompt: How many clock ticks lie strictly between vertex 1 discovery and finish?
quiz.explanation: Vertex 1 encloses the discovery and finish of its child 2, giving two interior ticks.

quiz.prompt: Which completed directed destination is a forward edge from u?
options: A vertex in a separate completed branch
quiz.explanation: The descendant interval lies strictly inside u's interval; another finished branch instead gives a cross edge.

examQuestions.question: Give a correctness proof for Depth-First Search. Explain the assumptions and termination.
examQuestions.answerHtml:
During a DFS call, every active vertex is on the current recursion path. A newly called vertex was white, so a vertex cannot create a second active call for itself. This discovery rule prevents infinite recursion around cycles. Each call has a finite neighbour list and eventually returns.

If an edge leaves a discovered vertex toward a white neighbour, DFS follows it before that vertex finishes. Suppose some reachable vertex stayed white after the root returned. Along a path from the root, take the first white vertex. Its predecessor was explored and should have followed that edge, which is a contradiction.

In an undirected graph, one root therefore visits exactly one connected component. No edge can lead into another component by definition. examQuestions.question: Derive the time and auxiliary-space bounds of Depth-First Search, distinguishing representation and working storage.
examQuestions.answerHtml:
DFS gives each vertex one discovery event and one finish event. Its neighbour loop runs once per stored arc. Across a full forest, the work is O(V+E). Reading the graph, assigning zero times and trying all outer roots also fits this bound for adjacency-list storage.

The discover, finish and comp arrays use O(V) space. In the worst case, a chain puts V calls on the recursion stack before any returns. That stack must be included, even though the source code contains no explicit stack array. Graph storage adds O(V+E) when lists reserve only used arcs.

The six-node C demonstration reserves six neighbours per vertex and builds those lists from a bounded edge set. Its traversal still scans only actual degrees. If you replace lists with a full V by V matrix, scanning every possible neighbour makes DFS O(V²), even on a sparse graph.
